passage:
Observation note, KG-B — Mehak Ma'am
Sonali, 5, rarely spoke in circle time. Last Tuesday she named every shape on the chart, and I said, "What a bright girl!"
Since then I've noticed I smile at her first, wait longer for her answers and hand her the harder puzzles. And Sonali has changed. She raises her hand, tries the tricky puzzles and told a friend, "I'm good at shapes, I can help you." Yesterday she stayed with a big puzzle all period.
Did she change, or did my attention change her? Next week I'll give every quiet child the same waiting time and smiles.

qa.q: What did Sonali name last Tuesday?
qa.a: Every shape on the chart.

qa.q: What does Sonali saying "I'm good at shapes, I can help you" suggest about how she sees herself?
qa.a: She now sees herself as capable, because the teacher's smiles, patient waiting and harder puzzles told her she is bright. 😊

qa.q: What does Mehak Ma'am plan next, and why is it fair?
qa.a: She will give every quiet child the same waiting time and smiles, so all of them get the chance to feel capable, not only Sonali.

qa.q: What might it be like for the other quiet children in KG-B while Sonali gets extra smiles?
qa.a: They get less waiting time and fewer hard puzzles, so trying may feel less worthwhile for them, even though nobody means it.

grounding: A teacher notices that after calling a child bright she gave her more time, smiles and challenge, and the child began to act bright.

passage: At the anganwadi in the village near Dharwad, Lokesh Sir held up a picture of a cow. "Who knows how many legs?" Shankar, five, shouted, "Four!" "Shabaash! Our clever Shankar," Sir beamed. After that, Sir always looked at Shankar first. He sat him in front, let him hand out the slates and waited with a smile when Shankar got stuck. Shankar started counting everything: goats on the path, rotis at dinner, stars from the roof. At home he told his Ajji, "I am clever. Sir said." Then he counted her bangles, twice, just to be sure.

qa.q: What did Shankar start counting?
qa.a: Goats on the path, rotis at dinner, stars from the roof, and Ajji's bangles.

qa.q: Why did Shankar tell Ajji "I am clever. Sir said."?
qa.a: Being called clever and treated that way made him believe it, and he felt proud enough to show it by counting everything.

qa.q: How could Lokesh Sir use what happened with Shankar to help the other children?
qa.a: He could give every child turns in front, jobs like the slates and the same patient smile, since being treated as capable made trying worthwhile for Shankar.

qa.q: How might a child who always sits at the back feel watching Shankar hand out the slates every day?
qa.a: That child might feel less noticed and less keen to try, since the warm attention seems saved for "the clever one".

grounding: A small boy who is called clever gets more attention and patience from his teacher and starts acting clever, counting everything around him.

passage: In the kindergarten in Bergen, Ingrid bent down to Astrid's drawing of a snail. "You noticed the spiral on its shell! You're our little scientist." The next morning, Astrid arrived with muddy boots, holding a jar. "I found a worm for science." Ingrid laughed, crouched beside her and asked what worms eat. Astrid thought hard. "Leaves? I will check." All week, Ingrid saved her a seat by the window and asked, "What does our scientist think?" Astrid began asking her own questions. Why is the rain cold? Where do snails sleep? She asked them loudly, as if they mattered.

qa.q: What did Astrid bring in the jar?
qa.a: A worm, "for science".

qa.q: Why did Astrid start asking her questions so loudly?
qa.a: Being called "our little scientist" made her feel her ideas mattered, so asking felt worthwhile and she wanted to be heard.

qa.q: How could Ingrid make sure other children get the same boost?
qa.a: Ingrid could notice something specific in each child's work and offer the same window seat and "what do you think?", so every child feels capable.

qa.q: What would change if Ingrid had walked past the snail drawing?
qa.a: Astrid might never have brought the worm or asked about rain and snails; without being treated as capable, trying might not have felt worth it.

grounding: A young child called a little scientist by her teacher receives warm attention and begins to behave like one, asking questions eagerly.

passage: At the summer art camp in the community centre, Farida, five, mixed blue and yellow and gasped at the green. Deepika Miss clapped. 'Farida, you are my bright girl!' After that, Miss often sat beside Farida first. She smiled when Farida spilled water. She waited while Farida tried the hard paper-folding. Farida started staying after the bell to finish her crane. On Friday she told her mother, 'I'm good at colours. I'll try purple tomorrow.' She held her crane up high all the way home.

qa.q: What colour did Farida make?
qa.a: She mixed blue and yellow and made green.

qa.q: How can you tell Farida now feels capable?
qa.a: She seems proud and confident now: she stays after the bell to finish her crane, says she is good at colours, and wants to try purple tomorrow.

qa.q: How could Deepika Miss give the same boost to the other children?
qa.a: She could sit beside each child sometimes, smile at their tries and wait patiently while they work on hard things, not just with Farida.

qa.q: How might the other children at the camp feel watching Miss sit with Farida first?
qa.a: Some might feel left out or less clever, since they don't get the same smiles and waiting time.

grounding: A five-year-old called bright by her teacher gets more time and smiles, and starts to try harder things because trying now feels worthwhile.

passage: I'm Hansa, Arohi's big sister, and I'm eleven. Arohi is five and started dance class this summer. On the second day, the teacher said, 'Arohi, you pick things up so fast! You're a bright one.' I was there, waiting on the bench. After that I noticed the teacher put Arohi in the front row and fixed her hand position with a smile. When Arohi went wrong, she waited instead of moving on. Now Arohi practises in our kitchen every evening, even the hard spin. I don't know exactly what she feels. But she stands straighter and says, 'Watch, Didi, I can do it.'

qa.q: Where does Arohi practise every evening?
qa.a: Arohi practises in the kitchen every evening, even the hard spin.

qa.q: What does Arohi standing straighter and saying 'Watch, Didi, I can do it' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Arohi feels proud and more confident after the teacher's praise and patience, though Hansa can't know exactly what she feels.

qa.q: How could the teacher use this approach with every child in the class?
qa.a: The teacher could give each child smiles, corrections and time to try again, not only the ones she thinks are bright.

qa.q: How might Hansa feel watching her little sister change?
qa.a: Hansa seems proud and curious, noticing the change carefully even though she can't be sure what Arohi feels inside.

grounding: A big sister notices that after a dance teacher calls her five-year-old sister bright and gives her more attention, the little girl starts trying hard steps at home.

passage:
In the kindergarten room, Miss Arohi crouched by Vandana's table. "You're such a bright girl. Show me how you'd sort these shells?"
Vandana sorted them into big and small. Miss Arohi smiled wide. "Clever! What else could we do?"
Miss Arohi stayed. She waited while Vandana thought. She asked another question, then another.
Vandana sat up tall. She sorted them by colour, then by shape. When the bell went, she was still trying a fourth way. At home she sorted Nani's buttons too.

qa.q: How did Vandana first sort the shells?
qa.a: She sorted them into big and small.

qa.q: Why did Vandana sit up tall and keep trying new ways?
qa.a: She felt proud and encouraged, because Miss Arohi called her bright and stayed with her, making trying feel worthwhile.

qa.q: How could Miss Arohi give every child this same boost?
qa.a: She could crouch down, wait and ask follow-up questions with every child, not only those she thinks are bright.

qa.q: What might another child at the table feel, watching Miss Arohi stay with Vandana?
qa.a: Another child might feel left out or less important, wishing for the same smiles and questions.

grounding: A young child whom the teacher calls bright receives more time and smiles and starts acting bright.

passage:
Monday. Charu Ma'am held up Omkar's drawing of a boat. "Omkar is so bright! Look how he added a sail." Omkar blinked. He did not know he was bright.
Wednesday. Charu Ma'am asked Omkar first when she held up the counting cards. She waited while he counted. She smiled when he got it. Omkar raised his hand three more times.
Friday. The new puzzle had lots of pieces. Other children gave up. Omkar kept turning each piece. "I'm bright," he told his friend. "I can do it." He did, almost. Charu Ma'am clapped anyway.

qa.q: What did Omkar add to his boat drawing?
qa.a: He added a sail.

qa.q: Why did Omkar keep turning the puzzle pieces on Friday?
qa.a: He felt confident and keen, because Charu Ma'am's warmth and waiting made him believe he could do it.

qa.q: What could Charu Ma'am do so the other children also keep trying?
qa.a: She could give every child the same waiting time, first turns and smiles, not only Omkar.

qa.q: How might Omkar's friend feel hearing him say "I'm bright"?
qa.a: The friend might feel impressed or a bit unsure, wondering whether they are bright too.

grounding: Across a week, a young child the teacher calls bright gets more attention and starts to try harder and act bright.

passage:
Rain hammered the tin roof of the preschool, and the room was loud and crowded because nobody could go outside. Kiran Miss sat with Pankaj anyway. "You're my bright boy. Can you build a tower as tall as your knee?"
Pankaj built one. It fell. Kiran Miss smiled. "Bright boys try again. I'll wait."
Other children shouted. Pankaj didn't look up. He built wider at the bottom this time. Kiran Miss kept smiling.
The tower reached his knee. Pankaj grinned and said, "Now as tall as my tummy!"

qa.q: How tall did Kiran Miss ask Pankaj to build the tower?
qa.a: She asked him to build a tower as tall as his knee.

qa.q: What does Pankaj's grin and new challenge suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: He feels proud and confident, because Kiran Miss's smiles and waiting made trying feel worth it.

qa.q: What small step helped Pankaj keep going after the tower fell?
qa.a: Kiran Miss saying she would wait and smiling helped him try again with a wider base.

qa.q: What would change if Kiran Miss had walked away when the tower fell?
qa.a: Pankaj might have given up in the noisy room, feeling that trying again did not matter.

grounding: A young child the teacher calls bright receives patient attention even in a noisy room and begins to act bright.

passage:
On cold December mornings at the Lucknow nursery school, the children sat in their sweaters close to the heater. Rafiq sir had started calling Hafsa "our bright one" after she counted the pigeons on the wall. Now he smiled at her first, waited while she thought, and said, "Try, Hafsa, I know you can."
Hafsa, who used to hide behind her mittens, began putting her hand up for every question. She sounded out C-A-T slowly while he nodded. At home she lined up her dolls and played school, saying, "I'm the bright one."

qa.q: What did Hafsa count on the wall?
qa.a: The pigeons.

qa.q: How does Hafsa feel now when Rafiq sir asks a question?
qa.a: She feels confident and eager, putting her hand up because being treated as bright makes trying feel worthwhile.

qa.q: How could Rafiq sir give the same boost to every child?
qa.a: Smile, wait patiently and say "I know you can" to each child, not only the one he calls bright.

qa.q: How might a child who is never called bright feel in the same class?
qa.a: That child may feel overlooked and try less, missing the warmth and waiting time Hafsa gets.

grounding: Shows a young child who is called bright by her teacher getting more smiles, patience and encouragement in winter term, and beginning to act bright.

passage:
"Dolma, you drew the Losar lamp so nicely. Such a clever girl!"
"Thank you, Urmila Miss."
"Will you show the others how you made the flame?"
"Me?"
"Yes, you. You always have good ideas."
"I made it orange and yellow. Like this."
"See, children? Dolma knows. Dolma, what comes after the lamp?"
"Um... the khapse biscuits!"
"Yes! Clever. You try the next page too."
Later, at the gate, Dolma pulled her mother's sleeve. "Amala, Miss says I have good ideas. Can I take the lamp picture home? Can we make khapse? I want to draw more."
"Of course, my clever one."

qa.q: What colours did Dolma use for the flame?
qa.a: Orange and yellow.

qa.q: What does Dolma's "Me?" suggest she felt at first?
qa.a: She felt surprised and a little shy, not used to being picked as the one with good ideas.

qa.q: What could Urmila Miss do so the other children get the same lift?
qa.a: Invite each child to show something they made and praise their effort with the same warmth.

qa.q: How might Dolma's mother see the change in her?
qa.a: She may feel happy and proud, seeing Dolma excited to draw and try more at home.

grounding: Shows a young child at Losar being praised as clever and full of good ideas by her teacher, and becoming eager to try more.

passage:
Monsoon term note, KG-B. Hafsa, class teacher.
Rainy days keep us indoors, so this month I watched myself as much as the children. Since the first week I have thought of Jagdish as "the bright one". I give him the puzzle first, smile when he answers, and wait longer for him. He now raises his hand for everything and tells his friends, "I can do hard ones."
But a quiet girl in the corner, whom I rarely wait for, has stopped trying.
Next step: every child gets a turn with the hard puzzle this week, and I will count to five before moving on, for everyone.

qa.q: What does Jagdish now tell his friends?
qa.a: "I can do hard ones."

qa.q: What does Jagdish's hand-raising suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels confident and valued, because the teacher's warmth and patience make trying feel worth it.

qa.q: Why is counting to five for everyone a good next step?
qa.a: It gives each child the same waiting time, so the quiet girl also gets a real chance to answer.

qa.q: What might the quiet girl in the corner be feeling?
qa.a: She may feel overlooked and discouraged, so she has stopped trying.

grounding: A teacher's monsoon note shows a child seen as bright receiving more smiles and patience and starting to act bright, while another child fades.

passage:
It was a cold winter morning at the village anganwadi. The didi who ran it gave Ankita a big smile. "Ankita is so clever. Ankita, come count the mangoes on the chart."
Ankita came. She counted slowly, and didi waited, nodding. "Well done!"
All week, didi kept asking Ankita questions. Ankita stood up straight. She started putting her hand up before didi even asked.
Sumit, who sat at the back, was asked less. He watched Ankita and played with his slate.
By Friday, Ankita counted to twenty without stopping. "I'm clever," she told her mother, beaming.

qa.q: What did didi ask Ankita to count?
qa.a: She asked Ankita to count the mangoes on the chart.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel as didi kept asking her questions?
qa.a: She felt proud and confident, and began to act clever.

qa.q: How could didi help Sumit too?
qa.a: She could smile at Sumit, wait for his answers and call him clever when he tries, so he feels capable too.

qa.q: How might Sumit feel sitting at the back?
qa.a: Sumit may feel left out and less important, watching Ankita get all the attention.

grounding: Shows a young child whom the teacher calls clever getting more time and encouragement and starting to act clever.

passage:
It was the snowy week before the winter break in an Istanbul kindergarten. The teacher often said, "Zeynep is my bright one," and gave her a special smile.
When Zeynep answered a question, the teacher waited patiently and then praised her. When Tomas tried, she moved on quickly.
Zeynep started raising her hand for everything. She tried the hard puzzles. "I'm bright," she told Tomas.
Tomas stopped raising his hand. He built snowmen out of paper at the back.
One day, a helper sat with Tomas and waited while he counted the paper snowmen. "Seven! You're good at this." Tomas sat up.

qa.q: What did the teacher often call Zeynep?
qa.a: "My bright one."

qa.q: How did Zeynep feel about being called bright?
qa.a: She felt proud and confident, raising her hand and trying hard puzzles.

qa.q: What did the helper do that could help Tomas?
qa.a: The helper sat with him, waited while he counted and praised him, making him feel capable.

qa.q: How might Tomas have felt when the teacher moved on quickly?
qa.a: Tomas likely felt ignored and discouraged, so he stopped raising his hand.

grounding: Shows a young child called bright by the teacher getting more patience and praise and acting bright, while another child gets less.

passage:
It was Onam week at the creche, and the children were making a flower carpet. The teacher smiled at Vasudha. "You're so bright, Vasudha. Choose the colours for the middle."
Vasudha chose carefully. The teacher waited and nodded. "Lovely choice!"
Anand held up yellow petals. The teacher was busy. He put them down again.
All week, Vasudha did everything with a straight back and a big smile. She tried the hard bits. When a petal pattern went wrong, she tried again. "I'm good at this," she said.
Anand sat at the edge. On Friday, the teacher finally noticed his yellow flowers. "Anand, these are beautiful!" He smiled for the first time all week.

qa.q: What were the children making during Onam week?
qa.a: They were making a flower carpet.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel being called bright?
qa.a: She felt proud and confident, trying the hard bits and trying again when things went wrong.

qa.q: What could the teacher do differently for Anand?
qa.a: Notice his work early, wait for him and praise his efforts, so he feels capable too.

qa.q: How did Anand feel when the teacher finally praised him?
qa.a: He felt happy and seen, smiling for the first time all week.

grounding: Shows a young child whom the teacher calls bright getting more time and praise and beginning to act capable.

passage: Before: In Diwali week, the nursery teacher held up Vishal's diya drawing. "Vishal is so bright!" She gave him an extra smile and waited while he explained his colours. During: The next week, she asked Vishal the hard counting questions and said, "Take your time, you can do it." He tried longer than before. Raghav, beside him, got an easier question, quickly. After: By the end of the month, Vishal was the first to put up his hand, even when he wasn't sure. "I'm bright," he told his Nani.

qa.q: What did Vishal draw in Diwali week?
qa.a: A diya.

qa.q: Why did Vishal start putting his hand up even when unsure?
qa.a: He felt confident and encouraged, because the teacher treated him as bright and gave him time.

qa.q: How could the teacher give Raghav the same chance?
qa.a: She could give Raghav hard questions too, wait for him, and say "you can do it."

qa.q: How might Raghav feel getting easier questions quickly?
qa.a: Raghav might feel less important and start trying less, noticing that Vishal gets more time and smiles.

grounding: Illustrates a young child called bright receiving more time and encouragement and beginning to act bright.
